text: Cells are the basic units of life. Every living thing is made of one or more cells. Some living things, like bacteria, have only one cell. People have trillions of cells. Each cell has a thin outer layer called the membrane. Inside, many cells have a nucleus that holds the instructions for the cell. Cells take in food, use energy and make new cells.

Force is a push or a pull. When you kick a ball, your foot pushes it and it moves. Friction is a force that slows things down. A ball rolls farther on smooth ice than on grass, because grass has more friction. Gravity is a force that pulls things toward the Earth. That is why a ball falls back down when you throw it up.

A map is a drawing of a place seen from above. Maps use symbols to show roads, rivers and towns. A compass rose shows north, south, east and west. The scale tells how far one part of the map is in real life. People use maps to plan trips and to find their way. Today many maps are on phones and computers.

Matter is anything that takes up space and has mass. Matter can be a solid, a liquid or a gas. Ice is a solid. When it warms up, it melts and becomes liquid water. If water gets very hot, it boils and becomes a gas called steam. When steam cools, it turns back into water.

Sound is made when things shake, or vibrate. When you hit a drum, the top of the drum shakes. The shaking moves the air, and the moving air reaches our ears. Fast vibrations make high sounds. Slow vibrations make low sounds. Sound can travel through air, water and even solid walls.

The Earth turns around once every day. When our side of the Earth faces the sun, it is day. When it faces away from the sun, it is night. The Earth also moves around the sun. One trip around the sun takes about one year. The tilt of the Earth gives us the seasons.
